notes.meaning: Paul tells Titus to keep reminding believers to respect and obey government leaders. Christians should live as good citizens and be ready to do every kind of good work. They obey the laws of the land unless doing so would force them to disobey God.

Believers must not speak evil of anyone or pick fights. Instead, they should be gentle, patient, and considerate toward every person they meet. This humble kindness shows the love of Christ to an unbelieving world.

Paul explains why Christians must be patient with outsiders. Before coming to Christ, believers were just as foolish, trapped by sinful desires and full of envy and hatred. Remembering their own past keeps them from looking down on other people.

Everything changed when God revealed His great kindness and love toward the human race. People did not take the first step toward God; He reached down to rescue them while they were still lost in sin.

God did not save us because of any good deeds we had done, since our own works could never earn His favor. He saved us purely out of His mercy, giving us a fresh start and new life through the Holy Spirit.

differ.view: Baptists teach that the washing does not refer to water baptism, because salvation comes only by inward faith and the work of the Holy Spirit.
Lutherans teach that the water of baptism is the washing of new birth, through which the Holy Spirit creates faith and gives new life.
Presbyterians and Reformed Christians teach that baptism is an outward sign and seal of the Spirit's inward work, not the power that saves.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that baptism is the sacrament that washes away sin and causes spiritual rebirth.

notes.meaning: God did not hold back when giving the Holy Spirit, but poured Him out richly on believers. This generous gift comes entirely through Jesus Christ, who made peace between God and sinners.

God justified believers—meaning He declared them right with Him and pardoned their sins—solely by His free grace, not because of their own merit. As a result, Christians are welcomed into God's family and have the confident hope of living with Him forever.

Paul calls this truth about God's free salvation completely trustworthy and tells Titus to preach it with confidence. When believers understand how deeply God has loved them, they will naturally devote themselves to doing good deeds. These good actions help other people and honor God.
Titus must steer clear of pointless arguments, useless debates over family trees, and squabbles about the Jewish law. These arguments produce no spiritual fruit and only end up wasting time.

If someone keeps stirring up divisions and building factions in the church, the leaders should warn that person once, and then a second time. If the troublemaker refuses to listen, the church must have nothing more to do with them.

Anyone who continues dividing the church after being warned is twisted and continuing in sin. Such people condemn themselves, because their own stubborn refusal to change proves they know they are doing wrong.

Paul plans to send either Artemas or Tychicus to take over Titus's work in Crete. Once that replacement arrives, Titus is instructed to travel quickly to meet Paul in Nicopolis, where the apostle has chosen to spend the winter.

Titus is told to take good care of Zenas the lawyer and Apollos as they prepare for their journey. The church is responsible to supply everything traveling workers need so their ministry is not hindered.

The believers in Crete must learn to put their faith into practice through honest work and by helping people with urgent needs. When Christians look out for others, their lives are fruitful rather than idle and empty.

Paul passes along warm greetings from everyone traveling with him and sends his love to all who share their Christian faith. He ends the letter with a prayer that God's grace will rest upon the whole congregation.
